lesson.title: Naming the Rule: How Function Notation Works
lesson.summary: Function notation, like f(x), is a compact way to name a function and show exactly which input it is being evaluated at, replacing clunkier equation forms with a clear, reusable label.
lesson.body:
Function notation is a shorthand for naming a function and showing precisely which input is being used. Instead of writing y equals some expression in x, function notation writes f(x) equals that same expression, replacing y with a label, f, followed by parentheses containing the input variable. The letter f is just a name, chosen the way you might name a variable; other common letters include g, h, and capital letters like P for a population function or C for a cost function. The parentheses do not mean multiplication here, which is a common early mix-up; f(x) is read aloud as f of x, meaning the output of function f when the input is x, not f times x.

The real power of function notation shows up when you want to describe a specific input without rewriting the whole rule from scratch. If f(x) = 2x + 5, then f(3) means evaluate this function at the input 3, which you calculate by substituting 3 everywhere x appears: f(3) = 2(3) + 5 = 6 + 5 = 11. The notation f(3) = 11 compactly records an entire ordered pair, (3, 11), input and output together, in a single, readable statement. Compare this to the older approach of writing y = 2x + 5 and then saying when x is 3, y is 11; function notation says the same thing in fewer symbols and makes clear exactly which function is being discussed, which matters once a problem involves more than one function at a time.

Work through a full example with two functions at once. Let f(x) = x^2 - 1 and g(x) = 4x. Find f(2) and g(2). For f(2), substitute 2 for x: f(2) = 2^2 - 1 = 4 - 1 = 3. For g(2), substitute 2 for x: g(2) = 4(2) = 8. Notice that the same input, 2, produces two completely different outputs, 3 and 8, because f and g are two different functions with two different rules. Without function notation, distinguishing the y-value from the first equation from the y-value from the second equation would be far clumsier to write and to talk about.

Function notation also connects directly back to relations and ordered pairs. Any statement f(a) = b is exactly equivalent to saying the ordered pair (a, b) belongs to the function f, with a as the input and b as the output. This means every skill you have already built, reading ordered pairs, identifying domain and range, and separating inputs from outputs, transfers directly into reading and writing function notation; nothing new is being invented, only a cleaner label is being attached to ideas you already understand.

Because function notation makes the input completely explicit, it becomes the standard language for the next skill in this unit, evaluating functions, where you will substitute numbers, and sometimes even expressions, into f(x) and simplify carefully using the order of operations you already rely on when evaluating any algebraic expression. Getting fluent at reading f(x) notation now will make every later course, from more advanced algebra through calculus, far easier to follow, since this same labeling convention is used everywhere functions appear.
